papers.version_note: arXiv:2510.19730v2, dated 19 Feb 2026; the text layer garbles most equations, so equations are not quoted.
papers.what_it_is: A theoretical and numerical paper from Quantum Computing Inc proposing encoding of information in the relative displacement or photon number of two optical modes (DiPNE and DiDE) and showing that photon subtraction can prepare high-fidelity superpositions of squeezed displaced states.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper does not propose a full paradigm for an analog optical quantum optimiser. It studies the encoding only, and does not fully describe the entropy computing paradigm.
quotes: In this work we do not propose a full paradigm for building an analog optical quantum optimiser
This paper studies one aspect of early entropy computers, the encoding.
We emphasize that this work does not fully describe the entropy computing paradigm, which will be discussed in forthcoming work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states the scope of the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that photon loss and its decohering effect are ignored throughout the work, and that this loss could have a major effect on performance in practice. They say the goal is to understand mathematically what could be possible, not to propose a full experimental paradigm.
quotes: throughout this work we ignore the decohering effect of photon loss, which in practice could have a major effect on performance.
The goal of this work is to mathematically understand what could be possible setting rather than propose a full experimental paradigm
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states this limit of the analysis.
assertions.reader_inference: All later results (fidelities, erasure, correction) hold in a lossless model; none is a statement about hardware with loss.

assertions.value: The authors define Differential Photon Number Encoding (DiPNE) as encoding a bit in the relative displacement, which relates to photon number, of two packets of fixed phase. The variable value is set by which mode has more photons. DiDE (Differential Displacement Encoding) is the closely related method based on measuring differential displacement.
quotes: We find that we can effectively encode a bit of information in the relative displacement (which in turn relates to photon number) of two packets of fixed phase, with the variable value determined by which mode has more photons.
We call this scheme Differential Photon Number Encoding (DiPNE), and a closely related method based on measuring Differential Displacement (DiDE).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 and Section 3 define the encodings.

assertions.value: The authors define a related encoding, differential displacement encoding (DiDE), that encodes a binary variable into relative displacement and can be measured by homodyne measurement. DiPNE is instead based on photon number measurements.
quotes: A related but distinct encoding is to rather encode a binary variable into relative displacement, which we will call differential displacement encoding (DiDE), which can be measured using homodyne measurement
DiDE (differential displacement encoding) is based on directly measuring field strength (mathematically represented by displacement).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 and the Fig. 1 caption define DiDE.

assertions.value: The authors state that an advantage of relative photon number over relative phase is that it extends easily beyond binary variables, for example to more than two modes, where the mode with the most photons gives the variable value.
quotes: An advantage of representing information in relative photon number as opposed to relative phase is that it is easy to extend beyond binary variables
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no multi-mode case is run.

assertions.value: The authors describe DiPNE as the converse of the coherent Ising machine encoding. It fixes the phase and encodes in displacement magnitude or photon number, where the coherent Ising machine encodes in phase. They state this is effectively what early entropy computing implementations do, with occupied time bins as variable values.
quotes: An interesting converse to the coherent Ising machine encoding is to instead encode into displacement magnitudes (or photon number), and to rather fix the phase for controllable interactions.
This is effectively the strategy employed in early implementations of entropy computing [15], with occupied bins corresponding to variable values in a time bin encoding.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of a relation to a cited entropy computing work, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors state that a beamsplitter translates between the phase encoding of a coherent Ising machine and the DiPNE or DiDE encoding. This holds as long as the local oscillator displacement exceeds the signal displacement, which fixes the relative phase. The translation is reversible because the beamsplitter unitary is self-inverse.
quotes: As long as |������LO| > |������������|, the relative phase is fixed, and the two modes can be made to be in phase by applying a −������ phase shift to the first mode.
Since the unitary operation that a beamsplitter performs is self-inverse, a translation in the other direction is also possible.
assertions.certainty_reason: Described in prose with the equation garbled in the text layer; the condition is quoted but the full derivation could not be quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the signal and local oscillator displacements have equal magnitude, one beamsplitter output is vacuum, and the condition for telling the two phases apart reduces to telling a coherent state from vacuum by photon counting.
quotes: one of the output modes of the beamsplitter will be vacuum and this condition collapses to the condition of distinguishability of a coherent state from vacuum by photon counting
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted; the distinguishability condition itself is a garbled equation in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dual-rail encoding used in protocols such as the KLM protocol can be viewed as a special case of DiPNE, with a single-photon number state in place of a coherent state, which allows complete distinguishability.
quotes: the dual-rail encoding which is used in protocols such as the famous KLM protocol [1] can be viewed as a special case of DiPNE encoding
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without a derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that coherent states used to store and process information cannot support a quantum advantage on their own, even with single-photon measurement, and that Gaussian boson sampling needs squeezing to become classically intractable. They state that coherent states alone cannot perform meaningful quantum computations because they have an efficient classical description.
assertions.anchor: Section 3, p.6; Section 5, p.10; Appendix B.1, p.22
quotes: which in itself, inherently, cannot support a quantum advantage, even with singlephoton measurement (even Gaussian Boson sampling requires squeezing to become classically intractable)
However, by themselves, coherent states cannot perform meaningful quantum computations, as they have an efficient classical description.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof in the main text; the background cites other work for related facts.

assertions.value: The authors state that for coherent states displaced in the same direction, DiPNE and DiDE are equivalent on average, and that the equivalence breaks for more general states: different squeezing in different modes can shift relative photon number without changing displacement. They say DiDE may be favoured when squeezing is strong and non-uniform.
quotes: Where the equivalence breaks down is for more general states of light.
Even when considering just Gaussian states, different levels of squeezing on the different modes can shift the relative photon number without changing the displacement.
so the DiDE may be favoured in cases with strong and non-uniform squeezing on different modes
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative argument; the squeezed-state photon number formulas are garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the outcome of homodyne measurements can be efficiently predicted for an entirely Gaussian system while photon number measurements cannot. They conclude that Gaussianity must be broken in another way when the DiDE encoding is used.
quotes: the outcome of homodyne measurements can be efficiently predicted for an entirely Gaussian system, while photon number measurements cannot (this is the essential idea behind Boson sampling).
This implies that when the DiDE encoding in 8 is used, Gaussianity must be broken in another way.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as background and consequence; no proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that with all modes in phase, a beamsplitter can pick off a small part of a pulse and interfere it with another pulse. Without an added phase shift there is more loss when both modes are occupied, and with a pi phase shift on the picked-off light the interaction favours both pulses having large displacement. The scheme can be applied symmetrically to the two modes.
quotes: one can use a beamsplitter to pick off a small portion of the light in a pulse, and then interfere this light with another pulse using a beamsplitter.
meaning that more loss will occur if both modes are occupied
then the interaction will favor both pulses having a large displacement
assertions.certainty_reason: Conceptual description of a circuit in Fig. 3; the phase symbol in the second case is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: For coherent states the paper derives the number of photons lost, which is a base term plus an interference term proportional to the real part of the product of one amplitude and the conjugate of the other, with sign set by the added phase shift. The authors state it holds for amplitudes in phase with each other, and that the interference favours less equal superpositions (antiferromagnetic coupling) in the plus case and more equal superpositions (ferromagnetic coupling) in the minus case.
quotes: In the case of coherent states, the number of photons lost can be calculated analytically.

The interference will then favor (in terms of the overall loss rate) less equal superpositions (effectively antiferromagnetic coupling) in the + case and more equal superpositions in the − case (effectively ferromagnetic coupling).

assertions.value: The authors state that because the covariance and displacement transform separately for Gaussian states, the change in average loss due to interference is independent of squeezing. They state similar arguments hold for many non-Gaussian distortions applied before displacement, as argued in appendix A.
quotes: since the covariance and displacement transform separately for Gaussian states [26], the modification of the average loss due to interference will be independent of squeezing.
Similar arguments can be made for many types of non-Gaussian distortions of the state which are performed before displacement, as argued mathematically in appendix A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued from a cited fact about Gaussian states; the paper does not state it as a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors report a full state space simulation of the interference gadget, with a maximum of thirty photons in each mode. They report that adding a photon to one or both modes, and adding squeezing, all give the same interference loss quantity as the vacuum case, in line with theoretical predictions.
quotes: Figure 4 confirms that all of these scenarios yield the same result, which is in line with theoretical predictions.
The numerical results were obtained through a full state space simulation with a maximum of 30 photons in each mode.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single numerical study run by the authors; results are shown only in the figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The check is a simulation of the authors own model, not an experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike the coherent Ising setting, the light picked off for interference needs to be compensated in the other mode, which can be done by taking the same amount of light from the pulse that does not take part in the interaction. They state an intentional imbalance can encode single-body terms.
quotes: the loss from picking off light for interference needs to be compensated in the other mode.
An intentional imbalance can be used to encode single-body terms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in prose as a conceptual remedy; not simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that for processing in superposition coherence must be kept, and that the light leaving the beamsplitter arm that does not encode a variable carries information on whether the Ising variables agree. They state that if this light is not treated carefully it could ruin any large-scale coherent superposition, and that this is a possible issue for both this encoding and the phase-based coherent Ising encoding.
quotes: the energy lost from the channel of the beamsplitter which does not continue will carry information about whether or not the Ising variables agree

assertions.value: The authors state that the combined displacement of the two pulses and the ratio between the more and less occupied pulse must be controlled when relative displacement encoding is used. They state this requirement may be lessened where the problem need not be represented at high precision, with maximum independent set given as the example, and that some correction may still be needed.

assertions.value: The authors propose that the total displacement and the magnitude of the difference between the two pulses can be measured by translating back to the phase encoding with the reverse translation circuit. The encoded value then maps to the phase of one output channel, and the two displacement quantities are the degrees of freedom to correct. They compare this to amplitude correction in a coherent Ising machine.

assertions.value: The paper proves, by counting terms in the beamsplitter expansion of two number states, that if the initial photon numbers on both inputs of a fifty fifty beamsplitter are odd, an equal number of photons cannot appear on each side after the beamsplitter. The authors state this implies that if one input holds a superposition of only odd photon numbers, the outputs cannot have equal numbers whatever the state in the other channel. They state the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect is the case with one photon in each input.

The Hong-Ou-Mandel effect represents the specific case with one photon in each input.

This further directly implies that if one input has a superposition of only odd photon numbers, the output numbers cannot be the same following interference with an arbitrary state of light in the other channel.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the fundamental components of a truly quantum analog optimiser with direct encoding, on a footing similar to a quantum annealer, exist, and that displacements provide a subspace allowing parallel computation. They state the loss that encodes the problem is insensitive to squeezing and to a large class of non-Gaussian fluctuations.
quotes: The conclusion is that the fundamental components for such an optimiser does indeed exist.
In particular, displacements provide a convenient subspace which allows for parallel computation.

assertions.value: The authors state that allowing some squeezing in the superposition lets standard kitten state preparation reach very high fidelity, usually above ninety nine percent and above ninety nine point nine percent in many cases, and that squeezing often accounts for less than ten percent of the photons. They suggest squeezing after preparation could standardize the displacements so more kitten states can be used.
